items.title: Adding nitro to benzene changes WHERE the next reaction happens
items.claim: Nitrate benzene to make nitrobenzene. Try to nitrate nitrobenzene again. The first nitro group already attached doesn't just slow the next reaction — it controls WHICH carbon the new NO2 goes onto, even at carbons it doesn't touch.
items.prompt: Where does the second NO2 go?

options.text: Predominantly meta to the first nitro group, because NO2 is electron-withdrawing and destabilises the carbocation intermediates at the ortho and para positions specifically
Predominantly ortho/para, because the existing nitro stabilises adjacent positive charge
The reaction does not proceed at all

items.reveal:
Electrophilic aromatic substitution goes through a sigma-complex (carbocation) intermediate. Draw the resonance structures of that intermediate for ortho, meta and para attack. For ortho and para attack, one resonance structure puts the positive charge directly on the carbon bearing the existing substituent.

If that substituent is electron-donating (like OH or NH2), it stabilises that positive charge — so ortho/para wins. If it's electron-withdrawing (like NO2), it destabilises that positive charge — so ortho/para becomes UNfavourable, and meta is by default the least bad option.

This sub-ring-level energetics translates into hard rules students learn as 'meta directors versus ortho/para directors'.
items.why: Directing effects look like an arbitrary memorisation list. They are direct consequences of intermediate stability — derivable from first principles.

items.title: Diamond does not conduct — graphite does
items.claim: Both diamond and graphite are pure carbon. Diamond is an insulator; graphite conducts electricity along its sheets. Same element, same atoms — wildly different electrical behaviour.

options.text: Graphite is impure and the impurities carry charge

Each carbon in graphite is sp2 with one p-electron contributed to a delocalised pi system spread across the entire sheet — these electrons are mobile and conduct, while diamond's sp3 carbons keep every electron locked in sigma bonds
Graphite ionises into C+ and C- pairs

items.reveal:
Diamond: every carbon is sp3, with four single bonds to neighbours. All valence electrons are in localised sigma bonds. No mobile carriers. Band gap is about 5.5 eV — diamond is an excellent insulator, almost transparent to visible light.

Graphite: each carbon is sp2. Three sigma bonds in the plane, one p-orbital perpendicular. Those p-orbitals overlap across the whole sheet, forming continuous pi bands. The bands are half-filled, like a 2D metal.

Graphene (a single graphite sheet) was isolated by Geim and Novoselov in 2004 and won them the 2010 Nobel Prize. Its electrons behave like effectively massless particles — a result of the band structure.
items.why: Element identity is taught as the main determinant of properties. Structure and bonding can change everything for the same atom.
